turns.reply: That's fair, it's a lot of new stuff. Do you want to stop here, do one more quick thing, or switch to the slides?

Thanks, just one quick thing. Look at the diagram: a fixed resistor at constant temperature gives a perfectly straight line. That tells us its resistance stays constant. What shape is the line on the diagram?
turns.diagramCaption: A resistor at constant temperature: a straight line through the origin.

turns.reply: Resistance is how hard it is for current to get through something, like a narrow, crowded corridor that slows people down. And the line on the diagram is a straight line. That was the quick one. Do you want to stop here, or keep going?

Let's go. A fixed resistor at constant temperature always has the same resistance, so we call it an ohmic conductor. It's like a corridor that stays the same width, whatever the crowd does.

If its resistance stays the same, what happens to the current when you give it a bigger push?
That's fair, it's a lot of new stuff. Do you want to stop here, do one more quick thing, or switch to the slides?

Thanks for sticking with it. For an ohmic conductor the current is directly proportional to the push, meaning doubling the push doubles the current.

If you double the push across a fixed resistor, what happens to the current?

Directly proportional just means that when one thing doubles, the other doubles too, like twice as many apples costing twice as much. So if you double the push across a fixed resistor, the current doubles as well. That was the quick one. Do you want to stop here, or keep going?

Let's keep going. A variable resistor is one where you change the resistance by hand, like the dial on a dimmer switch or a volume control. Turning it changes how hard it is for current to get through.

If you turn a dimmer switch so the resistance goes up, what happens to the lamp's brightness?

Yes, dimmer is right: more resistance makes it harder for current to get through. Resistance is measured in ohms, which tell you how hard that squeeze is, like a narrower corridor.

If a lamp's resistance goes down, what happens to the current through it?

Yes — lower resistance means an easier path, so the current goes up. Look at the diagram: a diode is a component that lets current flow in one direction only, a bit like a one-way gate.

If current tries to go through a diode the opposite way, what do you think happens to it?
recap: Resistance is how hard it is for current to get through something.
A fixed resistor keeps the same resistance, so its graph is a straight line.
Double the push across it and the current doubles too.
Turn a variable resistor up and the lamp dims.
turns.diagramCaption: A diode: current flows in one direction only.

turns.reply: A diode is a small electronic part that works like a one-way door for current. Let it flow forwards and it goes through easily; push it backwards and the diode has a very high resistance, so only a tiny bit gets through. If you push the wrong way, what do you think you'd feel?
Sorry, that was a lot. An LED is a diode that glows, like a tiny bulb, when current flows forwards. What do you think an LED gives out?
LED stands for light-emitting diode. When current flows forwards through an LED, what do you think it gives out?
Yes — light is right, an LED gives out light. Now an LDR is a part whose resistance falls as the light gets brighter, as the diagram shows. In a bright room, what happens to the LDR's resistance?
recap: A diode lets current flow in one direction only, like a one-way door.
Forwards, current passes easily; backwards, its resistance is very high.
Backwards, only a tiny bit of current gets through.
An LED is a light-emitting diode that gives out light when current flows forwards.
turns.diagramCaption: An LDR: brighter light, lower resistance.

turns.reply: Yes — brighter light means the LDR's resistance goes down. A thermistor is similar but reacts to heat, not light: look at the diagram, hotter means lower resistance. What happens to a thermistor's resistance as a room gets colder?
recap: An LED gives out light, which is the opposite job to an LDR.
An LDR is a part that reacts to light.
Brighter light means the LDR's resistance goes down.
In a bright room, an LDR has low resistance.

turns.reply: Yes — colder means the thermistor's resistance goes up. That's the end of this lesson. You answered questions on LDRs and thermistors, and some on fixed and variable resistors and diodes, where I told you the rest. Nice work today.
recap: A thermistor's resistance changes with temperature.
Hotter means lower resistance, so colder means higher.
An LDR works the same way, but with light.
Brighter light means the LDR's resistance goes down.

turns.reply: Bye for now! You worked out how LDRs and thermistors react to light and heat, and that's the idea behind things like street lamps switching on at dusk. Come back any time to go over diodes again.
